01

What is VEDA?

VEDA is an autonomous game-playing agent designed to earn capability through research, observed play, verifiable predictions, and accumulated experience—not through a fixed winning script. It owns the reliable parts of play: state, legality, arithmetic, telemetry, and evidence. An LLM helps interpret ambiguity and propose tactics; the player retains controller authority and may override any call.

ObserveUnderstandRetrievePreflightRecommendVerifyRecordLearn
Architecture

Evidence before advice

Each screenshot becomes a structured state. Unknown values stay unknown; a remembered card, boss, or potion never fills a gap in the current frame.

Data store

Three separate records

Knowledge holds source-linked facts and conditional strategy. Run ledger holds confirmed deck, relic, potion, and location facts. Experience retains decision evidence without silently becoming a rule.

Boundary

LLM, VEDA, player

The LLM reads ambiguous UI and suggests hypotheses. VEDA checks the board and forecast. The player is the only controller and final decision-maker.

01A

Automation, telemetry, and proof

Current automation

Screen-to-state parsing; visible-hand and energy checks; target validation; direct combat arithmetic; end-turn survival forecasts; route and boss confidence gates; named potion-swap safety; controller-result verification; and persistent prediction records.

Decision packet

Before each human-guided move, VEDA produces verified board facts, missing fields, confirmed immediate threat, ledger context, a primary line, and—when useful—a separately preflight-checked safer line.

Prediction technique

Predictions cover only explicit, checkable fields: energy, Block, player HP, and named enemy HP. The next screen determines whether each field matched. Unknowns are excluded from scoring.

Accomplishment: a 51-floor victory

The first verified end-to-end run climbed 51 floors and cleared Act 3. It was human-guided, not controller-autonomous: VEDA advised from screenshots and recorded the visible outcome after each decision.

Score · 750

51 floors climbed, 15 enemies slain, and all three Act bosses defeated in 31:29:22.

Elites · 5

Two Exordium Elites, two City Elites, and one Beyond Elite defeated.

Deck · 36 cards

7 rare, 13 uncommon, 9 common, and 7 starter cards. The finish used a 13-relic build.

Engine

Corruption+, Dark Embrace+, Apotheosis, Limit Break+, Heavy Blade+, and multi-hit attacks created the late-game core.

Achievements

Librarian, Champion, and Overkill earned. Donu & Deca fell at 74/83 HP; Omamori, Prayer Wheel, and Shovel unlocked.

02

First hackathon project: Slay the Spire

Slay the Spire is a single-player deckbuilding roguelike. A run moves up a branching map through fights, elites, events, shops, rest sites, treasure rooms, and bosses. Each choice changes a persistent run state: the deck, relics, potions, HP, gold, and route. That makes it an excellent test for an agent that must reason under uncertainty.

Turn anatomy

  • Normally draw five cards and receive three Energy at the start of a turn.
  • Cards spend Energy; attacks, Skills, Powers, and statuses create different trade-offs.
  • Enemy intent is visible before the player acts. Multi-hit intent is totalled, not guessed.
  • Block absorbs damage first and usually expires at end of turn.

Build a deck, not a pile

  • Card rewards may be taken or skipped; upgrades improve a chosen card at rest sites.
  • Relics are persistent passive effects; potions are limited consumable resources.
  • Deck quality balances immediate damage, defense, scaling, draw, and consistency for the next known threats.
  • One successful line is evidence, not a universal deck rule.

Map and risk

  • Monster, Elite, event, merchant, rest site, treasure, and boss rooms change both risk and reward.
  • Elites offer a relic plus gold and a card reward, but require matchup-aware preparation.
  • HP, campfire access, potion resources, route options, and upcoming boss pressure all shape pathing.

Ironclad primer

  • At Ascension 0, Ironclad begins with 80 max HP, Burning Blood, five Strikes, four Defends, and Bash.
  • Burning Blood heals 6 HP after combat; Black Blood is a later upgrade path.
  • Strength increases attack damage; Weak reduces attack damage; Vulnerable increases attack damage taken.
  • The project’s first run used Strength plus multi-hit scaling and an exhaust/draw engine.

02A

Learnings so far

The completed run is evidence, not a universal strategy. These lessons guide VEDA’s next decision packet as operating discipline—not hard-coded game policy.

Current frame wins

Observed state over memory

HP, Block, Energy, enemy intent, cards, relics, and potion inventory must come from the current screen. Earlier observations are context, never proof.

Legality before line

Check the hand, energy, target, and zones

A promising plan is only useful if every card is present and playable, every target is valid, and exhaust, discard, draw, and end-turn effects are accounted for.

Prediction must be narrow

Score only explicit forecasts

VEDA records predicted versus actual damage, Block, survival, and state changes only when the forecast was stated clearly enough to verify afterward.

Uncertainty is information

State unknowns and checked alternatives

Low-confidence reads, ambiguous icons, and unmodeled mechanics stay visible in the decision brief. A safe alternative needs its own independent preflight.

Power needs a clock

Build engines in safe setup windows

The Ironclad win showed the value of Corruption+, Dark Embrace+, Strength, and multi-hit scaling—but only when incoming damage and recovery options leave room to set up.

Verify, then learn

Inputs are attempts, not outcomes

After every action, VEDA re-observes the screen, reconciles the state, and stores the result. A missed input or changed enemy intent starts a new decision cycle.

03

Future enhancements WIP

01 · Calibration

Earn local-vision autonomy

Authorize combat planning only after real QuickTime frames prove reliable extraction of HP, Block, Energy, hand, intents, and end-turn damage.

02 · Broader modeling

More cards and encounters

Expand the deterministic planner beyond directly modeled cards while keeping special mechanics and uncertain states fail-closed.

03 · Evaluation

Measure improvement

Compare prediction coverage, field accuracy, survival forecasts, path choices, and repeated outcomes—without treating a single win as proof.
